pr_body:
- This optional service lets consumers query to see if a service is resolvable without side effects (not having to explicitly resolve the service).
- Added new spec tests to verify the baseline behavior based on IServiceCollection features.

Fixes #53919

issue_context.title: Add ability to detect if a service is registered in the DI container
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @eerhardt, @maryamariyan See info in [area-owners.md](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/area-owners.md) if you want to be subscribed.
Issue Details
## Background and Motivation We have a couple of scenarios where various components want to detect if a type is a registered/resolvable in the DI container without actually resolving the service (as this has side effects). See the following issues: - https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/46132 - This would allow the logic in ActivatorUtilities to pick the constructor based on what services are registered in the container. Today the logic is pretty broken. - https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/32737 - Minimal APIs want to be able to differentiate arguments to the method that are resolvable as services without explicit attributes. - https://github.com/microsoft/reverse-proxy/pull/915/files#diff-1d82d5e829d3ed9881a0e402a311fec7cca647fcf40d878e8f26d9886ab7ae9fR62 YARP - Wanted to enable diagnostic features based on what services where registered. ## Proposed API ```diff namespace Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection { + public interface ISupportServiceQuery + { + bool CanGetService(Type serviceType); + } } ``` ## Usage Examples ``` C# bool? HasServiceType(IServiceProvider sp) { return sp.GetService()?.CanGetService(typeof(T)); } ``` - Open generics supported by the container will always return true. e.g.: ```C# void Tests(IServiceProvider sp) { // Assuming the container supports Func and IEnumerable var supportsQuery = sp.GetRequiredService(); Assert.True(supportsQuery.CanGetService(typeof(Func))); Assert.True(supportsQuery.CanGetService(typeof(IEnumerable))); } ``` Null means we can't tell if the service is registered since `ISupportServiceQuery` is optional. ## Risks - Other DI implementations may not be able to support it @alexmg @tillig @pakrym @ENikS @ipjohnson @dadhi @seesharper
Author: davidfowl
Assignees: -
Labels: `api-suggestion`, `area-Extensions-DependencyInjection`, `untriaged`

I think that was just meant to be a bullet point that clarified "resolvable" vs "registered". If the container natively supports `Func<>` then any `Func<T>` would return true right?

> Func<T> would return true right?

I think, no. Funny enough that the
most containers may implement `IsResolvable` as `TryResolve<Func<X>>() != null`

> I think, no.

This is something we need to resolve. If I ask about any `IEnumerable<T>` I think it should return true for example. Otherwise it basically doesn't work for open generics. Same with `IOptions<T>`  in the case of generic host based apps.

> Funny enough that the
most containers may implement IsResolvable as TryResolve<Func<X>>() != null

I hope not as that would lead to the side effects that caused this to be created in the first place. If you actually resolve the instance 
then you have to worry about disposal (and async disposal).

Ok, just to be on the same page. And I will talk just about DryIoc.

- For open-generics you may only ask if they registered or not, because you cannot actually resolve something open.
- The `IEnumerable<>` and `Func<>`, etc. are wrappers in the DryIoc terms, and you may check if the specific wrapper is registered.
- Given the closed type X, you may ask if `IsRegistered<X>()` which does not automatically mean the X is resolvable (missing dependency, wrong lifestyle, etc.).
-  To check if X is resolvable without creating the instance the simplest robust way (closest  to how container will actually resolve things) will be `Resolve<Func<X>>(ifUnresolved.ReturnDefault) != null`. 
- There are other DryIoc specific ways to check resolvability as well (e.g check if container can create the final expression for X), so there is no blockers here.

You might want semantically different methods for IsRegistered(service type) and the “can resolve” method to differentiate between being explicitly registered and the container being able to “figure out” how to resolve the service type in some cases.

And rather than do this, can you instead use some kind of nullify service registration as a stand in instead of doing the branching logic based on container registrations? That’s always my recommendation to users over relying on magic constructor selection logic

> `return sp.GetService<ISupportServiceQuery>()?.CanGetService(typeof(T));`

Why this pattern vs. 

```C#
return (sp as ISupportServiceQuery)?.CanGetService(typeof(T));
```

It seems like the SerivceProvider should be the one answering the question - and not some service that I get from the ServiceProvider.

> This would be an optional service that could be implemented by a DI container implementation similar to ISupportRequiredService.

`ISupportRequiredService` follows the usage pattern I have above:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/86719086d9fa65e004763b85a8bb560ec505ec2b/src/libraries/Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions/src/ServiceProviderServiceExtensions.cs#L50-L53

`CanGetService(typeof(T))` can get complicated really quick. For example:
* Is it enough for the container to check if it is a POCO type and assume it could be resolved?
* Is it generic? Open, closed, constrained? (Each follows different rules)
* Should it check if there are any public constructors?
* Can any of the constructors be instantiated, in other words, satisfied with dependencies (how deep do you go into dependency graph )?
* How about now, after something else has been registered?

Where do you draw the line and define minimum criteria?

@davidfowl

I would strongly disagree with your risk assessment. If, for example, containers disagree on how deep dependencies are checked when calling `CanGetService(typeof(T))`, it creates incompatibility that is very hard to fix.

```C#
sp.GetService<ISupportRequiredService>()?.CanGetService(typeof(T));
```

This pattern provides a better composability. I may not want to implement the feature services on the core container because they require additional package dependency.

I would probably echo @eerhardt around adding the functionality in the same way as `ISupportRequiredService`, where the `IServiceProvider` is extended with additional interfaces.

At a conceptual level, if a component other than the `IServiceProvider` itself is responsible for stating whether that `IServiceProvider` can provide a service, that feels like a strange disconnect to me. It would be possible for someone to register their own `ISupportServiceQuery` service override, and give very strange results to the caller that don't match up with the service provider at all.

On the package dependency note, for Autofac we already have a separate library with the MS DI package dependency, and we could add an `ISupportServiceQuery` to our existing `AutofacServiceProvider` implementation fairly trivially.

>> You might want semantically different methods for IsRegistered(service type) and the “can resolve” method

> I think the only difference is with respect to the wrappers/factories whatever you want to call the open generic "things" that containers can manifest on the fly. I'm not sure that difference is observable in the scenarios I mentioned above

From an Autofac standpoint, we can tell you if something _is registered_ but we can't really tell you without trying to resolve _whether you can actually get it_. I think maybe it's just a naming thing - I would call it `IsRegistered` or something like that rather than `CanGetService` simply because of the `CanGetService` -> `GetService` implied naming relationship. "I can get it, but when I tried to get it I got an exception!"

> That's up to the people on this issue to define. I think usually we start with the minimum. I don't see anything fundamentally wrong with the questions you pose, we just need to make some decisions.

We could decide on the minimum, but what if a container performs more thorough magic than the baseline and succeeds where default container fails? Not an unreasonable scenario, I had one case like this with internal `CanResolve` in the service provider.  Another [example](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/50029#issuecomment-819329628).

This will break expected behavior and create two different paths of execution. This type of errors are absolutely impossible for the regular user, without ASP.NET code, to detect and fix.

> From an Autofac standpoint, we can tell you if something is registered but we can't really tell you without trying to resolve whether you can actually get it. I think maybe it's just a naming thing - I would call it IsRegistered or something like that rather than CanGetService simply because of the CanGetService -> GetService implied naming relationship. "I can get it, but when I tried to get it I got an exception!"

Done. I renamed it to `IsRegistered`. As long as it has the intended semantics, I'm flexible on naming. Wrappers like IEnumerable\<T\> and Func\<T\> (when closed) are registered even if they weren't explicit added.

@ENikS 

> We could decide on the minimum, but what if a container performs more thorough magic than the baseline and succeeds where default container fails? Not an unreasonable scenario, I had one case like this with internal CanResolve in the service provider.

I'm not sure how this would break based on the intended use cases. Supporting more than the default container is fine and what other containers do today (supporting less on the other hand is what is broken). This is what the specification tests are for. Can you clarify what the broken scenario is?

> Not an unreasonable scenario, I had one case like this with internal CanResolve in the service provider.
Another example would be behavior like this

Sounds like a missed test case. These happen but they don't mean we should stop and do nothing. They get fixed and we move on.

> For example, Unity can resolve structs (if they are not ref). It is the only container that does it. So, if constructor has struct parameter Unity will succeed, but default will fail. Other containers might have different peculiarities.

I don't know why that matters. If you're using unity, then you can resolve structs. That feature doesn't need to be in the base feature set.

>Done. I renamed it to IsRegistered.

To satisfy scenarios this type is intended for I think the semantics have to be similar to `GetService() != null` but without actual instantiation. The `IsRegistered` just muddies the water as `IEnumerable<IService>` (and other patterns provided by 3rd party containers) are not explicitly registered.

Agreed @pakrym. I like IsResolvable better than IsRegistered. I still think I like CanGetService best.

@eerhardt 

> It seems like the SerivceProvider should be the one answering the question - and not some service that I get from the ServiceProvider.

In addition to @dadhi's point on composability, there's also precedent here with IServiceScopeFactory.

> there's also precedent here with IServiceScopeFactory.

And there's also precedent the other way with `ISupportRequiredService`. 😉

> I can tell you that IComponent is registered. I can't really tell you that it's not actually resolvable because there's logic involved doing service location in an imperative fashion.

While true, I think this is unimportant when it comes to naming. What we really want is the container's best guess as to whether it can resolve a service without incurring the side effects that actually creating the service instance would entail.

Might the container actually fail to resolve something it claims is resolvable because of something it couldn't know until it tried to build it? Sure, but I don't think that's a big deal or a reason to change the name to IsRegistered.

> Point being - there's a significant difference between IsRegistered and IsResolvable.

Exactly, but I think we should drive this discussion with the unit tests https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/53919#issuecomment-857479162.

There are scenarios mentioned above and unit tests that reflect the expected behavior, lets choose the behavior based on that. What should each of these assertions do?

You could make any API name longer by calling out all the edge cases. We want to know without incurring side effects what types a container will return null from GetService for instead of returning an instance or throwing due to misconfiguration.

I think MEDI can do this and be right 100% of the time. (Am I wrong about this?) I understand there might be edge cases for other containers where you might know this with as much certainty, but is there a use case that really breaks hard with this interpretation?

Perhaps if we list criteria of what should be considered **resolvable** it would be easier to understand and decide?  
What would be the default set we will have to implement?
I'd like to take this to the next API review (Thursday and you should all join!) so lets agree on the semantics and worry about naming after we decide.

We don't care if GetService fails because there's broken dependencies. We care more about if its possible to resolve or not. The use cases above don't rely on GetService/GetRequiredSerice succeeding after a call to `CanGetService`. They are using that knowledge to filter out constructors or determine that something "is a service" because it was added to the DI container. 

The only place where this was fuzzy in my original proposal was wrappers/factories/open generics that would always return true when closed but weren't explicitly added the container (IEnumerable\<T\>, Func\<T\> etc)
What about the name `IsCandidateForResolution`.

> We don't care if GetService fails because there's broken dependencies.

OK, that counters the @halter73 viewpoint that

> We want to know without incurring side effects what types a container will return null from GetService for instead of returning an instance or throwing due to misconfiguration.

And there's the rub - either it's "we don't care if it's going to fail" vs "we care if it's going to fail." If we can answer that, this whole thing gets resolved. (Pun... intended?)

What are the details on that API review meeting? Depending on time and day job pressures, I'll try to be there.

Assuming there's no guarantee of resolution, I'm fine with anything like

- `IsRegistered`
- `HasRegistration` or `HasRegistrationFor`
- `IsCandidateForResolution`
- `CanTryResolve` or `CanTryResolution`
- `IsInContainer` or `IsInProvider`

I agree with @davidfowl's take on this, in that for the cases being discussed we care about whether it's registered or not, not knowing if for some reason the `GetService` call will fail. As pointed out by @tillig there are quite literally an infinite number of ways actually resolving a service might fail.

> The IsRegistered just muddies the water as IEnumerable<IService> (and other patterns provided by 3rd party containers) are not explicitly registered.

This is why I agreed with @pakrym and don't like "registered" in the API name. Yes, we are querying the registrations and not actually getting any service, but `CanGetService()` should return false when `GetService()` would return null, and return true otherwise.

Yes there are an infinite number of ways `GetService()` could throw after `CanGetService()` returned true, but that's not enough of a reason to rename  `CanGetService()` to `IsRegistered()` and muddying the waters about when this API should return true vs false.

From my understanding of the requirement here, what we're after is a way to ask:

 "Has someone/something previously expressed an **intent** to supply an instance of a given type from the container?"

Being able to answer that questions means that, if someone uses a type in a method, the (for example) ASP.NET Core routing engine can determine that it should ask the service provider for the instance, rather than trying to bind it from somewhere else (like the route).

In my mind, a user may express an intent to supply `MyCustomService`, the ASP.NET Core runtime may express an intent to supply `IOptions<T>`, and Autofac has expressed an intent to supply `IEnumerable<T>`.

As @tillig says (and as far as I can tell we all agree), it's unreasonable to define an API that will actually try to tell you whether you can **definitely** get an instance of a service back from a `GetService` call without errors, without actually doing the thing, but the described requirement doesn't require that level of accuracy, just an understanding of the aforementioned **intent**.

If that statement is true, then the names can perhaps be agreed later, but my vote is for a name that reflects verifying that intent, like `InProvider`, `SuppliedByProvider`, `AvailableAsService`, `IsService` or similar.

I would also be up for attending an API review meeting on this if someone can provide details (and the timezones work out).
I like IsService.

`ISupportServiceQuery.IsService(IEnumerable<T>)` is true if `ISupportServiceQuery.IsService(T)` is also true
